title: Board-specific phases
description: I'm thinking that we may want to have board specific phases at some point; for example, I may just want to work on a plan but not actually implement anything; in that case, I would want to skip a bunch of phases.  Maybe allowing phases to be skipped would make sense, as a board configuration.

Ideation:
Board-specific phases would let individual boards opt out of pipeline stages they don't need — a planning-only board stops after plan review, a board without ideation skips straight to planning. The debate across multiple rounds has converged around two competing framings: (1) `terminal_stage`, a board config field that halts the pipeline waterfall after a named stage, routing items to `final-human-approval` instead of continuing downstream; and (2) `active_phases`, a unified list (e.g., `['plan', 'spec', 'impl']`) that declares which of the three natural sub-pipelines run. Both approaches aim to avoid a risky up-front refactor by exploiting the existing sequential block structure in `_run_pipeline_impl` (phases.py:1473), where three blocks are already gated by stage checks: the planning loop (~line 1485), spec writing (~line 1578), and impl/test/review (~line 1615).

The `terminal_stage` approach is the most pragmatic for truncation use cases. It requires exactly one config field and one check per block boundary, leaves the data contract between phases intact (because stopping before a consumer phase means no consumer runs with empty inputs), and routes items to `final-human-approval` rather than auto-closing them, preserving the human checkpoint. Its critical weakness is that it only models stopping early — a board that wants to skip ideation and jump straight to planning cannot express this with `terminal_stage` alone. Adding a separate `start_stage` or `skip_phases` mechanism to cover this use case fragments the configuration model and introduces two orthogonal knobs with complex interactions.

The `active_phases` proposal attempts a unified solution by letting boards declare which blocks are active, covering both truncation and skipping simultaneously. However, this conflates block selection with entry-point routing in a way that reintroduces the data contract problem. Declaring `active_phases: ['impl']` means skipping both planning and spec writing, but the impl block consumes `impl_spec` and `test_spec` produced by spec writing — with those fields empty, the implementing phase produces garbage output. The proposal relies on items being pre-populated with the required data before entering the pipeline, which is a workflow assumption that is not currently enforced or well-supported.

The most defensible path forward is `terminal_stage` with `final-human-approval` routing for the truncation case, accepting that skipping early phases is out of scope for the initial implementation. The skip-early-phases use case requires either pre-populating data fields (a UI/workflow concern) or formalizing sub-pipeline data contracts first — both are non-trivial follow-on efforts. Implementing `terminal_stage` now delivers the highest-value use case (plan-only boards) with minimal code risk, while the broader phase coupling problem (planning exit logic entangled with downstream assumptions, spec writing as gatekeeper for impl) is left as a known limitation to be addressed before any recipe-based composition is attempted.
